mainTopic: How much do people mistake the time of day? Witnesses, the deadline for eating חמץ on ערב פסח, and mealtimes
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing a discussion about witnesses who disagree on the hour of an event: people never confuse day with night, or morning (sun in the east) with afternoon (sun in the west). The גמרא then quotes the משנה where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה disagree about how late on ערב פסח one may eat חמץ. It uses that משנה to challenge the error estimates of אביי, who answers that witnesses are careful while חמץ is for everyone. Next it tests רבא's larger estimates. It explains that the sixth hour is risky because the sun is overhead, and that the fifth hour is forbidden because of cloudy days, while the fourth hour is safe because it is everyone's mealtime. This leads to a ברייתא about who eats at each hour of the morning, which is reordered to match רב פפא. רב אשי then teaches that each תנא is consistent between עדות and חמץ, and that the earlier answers are real answers. Finally, רב שימי בר אשי rules that a disagreement about sunrise voids testimony, and the explanation of that ruling continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: People do not confuse day with night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why we do not allow for a mistake at the start of the day. Nobody mixes up daytime with nighttime.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, people do not make mistakes between day and night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer from the previous section. It explains why we do not worry that a witness confused the very start of the day with the night before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא allowed that witnesses can be off by a certain amount of time. Someone might ask why that error should not also stretch back past dawn into the night. The answer is that day and night look completely different, so that kind of mistake does not happen.

phrases.english: Rather, between day and night
phrases.notes: Continues an answer from the previous עמוד.

phrases.english: people do not err.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בֵּין יְמָמָא לְלֵילְיָא לָא טָעוּ אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a defense that began on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Common-sense observation about how people perceive time
steps.terutzMaskana: No allowance for error is needed across the line between night and day.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People do not confuse day with night.

steps.title: People do not confuse the fifth hour with the seventh
steps.stepSummary: Logic would suggest allowing even more room for mistakes later in the day. But the fifth and seventh hours cannot be confused, because the sun is in the east at five and in the west at seven.
steps.simpleTranslation: And by right we should give even more leeway at the later end. But at the fifth hour the sun is in the east, and at the seventh hour the sun is in the west.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a possible thought: maybe the room for mistakes should be even larger later in the day. It answers right away that the fifth hour and the seventh hour look clearly different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Morning and afternoon are easy to tell apart, because the sun is on opposite sides of the sky. So a witness who said 'fifth hour' cannot really have meant 'seventh hour.' This limits how big an error we can assume.

keyTerms.meaning: By right / logically it should be
Forward, toward the later part of the day

steps.whatToRemember: There are two limits on mistaking the time. People never confuse day with night, and they never confuse morning (sun in the east) with afternoon (sun in the west).

phrases.english: And by right we should give even more (leeway) at the later end,
except that at five (hours) the sun is in the east,
and at seven (hours) the sun is in the west.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְדִין הוּא דְּנִיתֵּיב לְקַמֵּיהּ טְפֵי, אֶלָּא שֶׁבְּחָמֵשׁ חַמָּה בַּמִּזְרָח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit, at the later end of the day, alongside the first limit at the start of the day.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Logic would suggest allowing even more room for error later in the day.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fifth and seventh hours cannot be confused, because the sun is on opposite sides of the sky.

steps.title: The משנה on when חמץ may be eaten
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה. רבי מאיר says one may eat חמץ through the whole fifth hour and burns it at the start of the sixth. רבי יהודה says one may eat through the fourth hour, leaves the fifth hour 'in suspension,' and burns at the start of the sixth.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: רבי מאיר says, one eats (חמץ) the whole fifth hour and burns it at the start of the sixth. רבי יהודה says, one eats the whole fourth hour, holds it in suspension the whole fifth hour, and burns it at the start of the sixth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the משנה about חמץ on ערב פסח. This is a setup: the next steps will use this משנה to test אביי's estimates of how much people mistake the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law, חמץ may be eaten until midday, which is the end of the sixth hour. Each תנא stops people earlier, because they might misjudge the time. The size of the early cutoff shows how big a mistake each תנא is worried about.

keyTerms.meaning: One holds it in suspension: may not eat it, but need not burn it yet
At the beginning of the sixth hour

steps.confusionAlert: Hours here are counted from the start of the day, so the 'sixth hour' ends at midday. The Torah prohibition starts only at midday. Everything earlier than that is an extra safety margin set by the חכמים.

phrases.english: We learned (in the mishna): Rabbi Meir says:
One may eat (leaven) the entire fifth hour,
and one burns it at the beginning of the sixth.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
One may eat the entire fourth hour,
and holds it in abeyance the entire fifth hour,
and burns it at the beginning of the sixth.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אוֹכְלִין כׇּל חָמֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the discussion of witnesses to the main topic of חמץ, so that the estimates of human error can be tested.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: eat through the fifth hour. רבי יהודה: eat through the fourth hour, suspend during the fifth. Both: burn at the start of the sixth.

steps.title: Challenge to אביי's view of רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: אביי said that according to רבי מאיר a person makes no mistake at all, or, in another version, only a tiny mistake. If so, רבי מאיר should allow eating חמץ through the sixth hour, or almost to its end.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to אביי's explanation of רבי מאיר, that a person does not err at all, let him eat through the whole sixth hour! And even according to the other version, that a person errs a tiny bit, let him eat until just before the end of the sixth hour!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אביי's earlier claim about how much time people mistake according to רבי מאיר. It points out that this claim does not fit רבי מאיר's ruling in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If people never misjudge the time, there is no need for any safety margin before midday. Then one could eat until the very end of the sixth hour. Even if people misjudge only slightly, the margin should be tiny, not a full hour as רבי מאיר requires.

keyTerms.meaning: A person does not err at all
Let him eat (a challenge: then he should be allowed to eat)

phrases.english: According to Abaye, in accordance with Rabbi Meir,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אֵין אָדָם טוֹעֶה וְלֹא כְּלוּם —
phrases.english: who said: a person does not err at all —
let him eat the entire sixth hour!
And according to that other version as well,
which says: a person errs a tiny bit —
let him eat until (just before) the end of the sixth hour!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאַבָּיֵי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר, דְּאָמַר: אֵין אָדָם טוֹעֶה וְלֹא כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the משנה just quoted to challenge אביי.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's estimate of human error according to רבי מאיר (none at all, or a tiny bit)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A zero or tiny error would need a zero or tiny safety margin. Yet רבי מאיר stops people a full hour before midday.

steps.title: Challenge to אביי's view of רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: אביי said that according to רבי יהודה a person errs by half an hour, or, in another version, by an hour and a bit. If so, רבי יהודה should allow eating until the middle of the sixth hour, or until the end of the fifth hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to אביי's explanation of רבי יהודה, that a person errs by half an hour, let him eat until the middle of the sixth hour! And even according to the version you said, that a person errs by an hour and a bit, let him eat until the end of the fifth hour!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes the same kind of challenge for רבי יהודה. אביי's numbers do not match the early cutoff רבי יהודה gives in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An error of half an hour needs only a half-hour margin before midday, so eating should be allowed until the middle of the sixth hour. An error of an hour and a bit means stopping a little before the end of the fifth hour. But רבי יהודה stops eating already at the end of the fourth hour. That is a margin of two hours, which is much bigger than אביי's numbers.

keyTerms.meaning: The middle of the sixth hour
An hour and a little bit

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה about חמץ shows how big a mistake each תנא fears. רבי מאיר fears about one hour, and רבי יהודה about two hours. Both are larger than אביי's estimates, so אביי's view is being challenged.
steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge sets up the next stage of the סוגיא, which must either defend אביי or give a different measure of how much people mistake the time. That measure affects both testimony of witnesses and the deadlines for חמץ.

phrases.english: And according to Abaye, in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda,
who said: a person errs by half an hour —
let him eat until the middle of the sixth hour!
And according to the other version as well, that you said:
a person errs by an hour and a bit —
let him eat until (just before) the end of the fifth hour!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַבָּיֵי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּאָמַר: אָדָם טוֹעֶה חֲצִי שָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the same challenge from רבי מאיר to רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's estimate of human error according to רבי יהודה (half an hour, or an hour and a bit)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These error sizes would permit eating until the middle of the sixth hour or the end of the fifth. Yet רבי יהודה forbids eating already after the fourth hour.

steps.title: Witnesses are careful, but חמץ laws are for everyone
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers the challenges the גמרא raised against him in Steps 4-5. People who testify are careful and precise, but the laws of חמץ apply to everyone, including careless people. That is why the רבנן add a bigger safety margin for חמץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: testimony is handed to careful people, but the laws of חמץ are handed to everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends his view against the challenges from the משנה. Small error margins fit testimony, but the bigger margins of רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה fit חמץ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי had said that witnesses make only a tiny error, so the rules for חמץ seemed too strict. Now he explains that the two cases are different. A witness comes to court only after checking the details carefully. The ban on חמץ, by contrast, must be kept by every ordinary person, so the רבנן protect people who are less careful.

keyTerms.meaning: Testimony given by witnesses in court

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general rule. How large a safety margin the רבנן set depends on who must keep the law. A law for everyone needs more room for error than a matter handled by careful experts.

phrases.english: (Rather,) Abaye said:
phrases.notes: "Rather" signals that the challenge is answered by a new distinction. The word is in parentheses because some texts omit it.

phrases.english: testimony is entrusted to the vigilant,
phrases.notes: Witnesses check carefully before they testify, so they rarely make big mistakes.

phrases.english: leaven is entrusted to all.
phrases.notes: Everyone must keep the laws of חמץ, even careless people, so a bigger margin is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two challenges the גמרא raised against אביי in Steps 4 and 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases (חילוק): testimony versus a law that applies to everyone
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The error margin assumed for witnesses should also set the margin for חמץ.
steps.terutzMaskana: Witnesses are careful, so they need only a small margin. The public is not, so חמץ gets a larger margin.

steps.title: If people err almost two hours, stop eating from the fifth hour
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's view of רבי מאיר. If a person can be off by almost two hours, then someone in the fifth hour might really be in the seventh hour, when חמץ is forbidden by Torah law. So eating should stop at the start of the fifth hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבא's explanation of רבי מאיר, who said a person can err by two hours minus a little bit: then from the start of the fifth hour one should not eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבא's explanation and asks why רבי מאיר allows eating during the fifth hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah forbids חמץ from the seventh hour. If people can be off by almost two hours, someone who thinks it is the fifth hour could really be in the seventh. So the margin seems too small.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him eat (with לָא: let him not eat)

phrases.english: And Rava, according to Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: Now the גמרא looks at רבא's explanation of the משנה.

phrases.english: who said: a person errs
by two hours less a bit —
phrases.notes: Slightly less than two full hours.

phrases.english: from the beginning of the fifth, let him not eat!
phrases.notes: Because the fifth hour could be confused with the seventh, when the Torah forbids חמץ.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves אביי's approach and tests רבא's explanation of רבי מאיר instead.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that, according to רבי מאיר, a person errs by almost two hours
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An error of almost two hours links the fifth hour to the seventh, which is forbidden by Torah law. So eating should stop at the start of the fifth hour, not the sixth.

steps.title: The sun's position tells morning from afternoon
steps.stepSummary: Nobody mixes up the fifth hour with the seventh. At the fifth hour the sun is in the east, and at the seventh hour it is in the west.
steps.simpleTranslation: At five the sun is in the east, and at seven the sun is in the west.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the fifth and seventh hours look clearly different in the sky, so no one confuses them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general error of almost two hours does not apply across noon. Morning and afternoon are easy to tell apart, because the sun moves from the east side of the sky to the west side. So the fifth hour is safe to eat in.

phrases.english: at five, the sun is in the east,
and at seven, the sun is in the west.
phrases.notes: Morning and afternoon cannot be confused.

steps.triggerLanguage: חָמֵשׁ חַמָּה בַּמִּזְרָח, וְשֶׁבַע חַמָּה בַּמַּעֲרָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 7, using the same sun logic from Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the error: the error does not cross between morning and afternoon
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An error of almost two hours could link the fifth hour to the seventh.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sun's clear position, east or west, prevents confusing these two hours.

steps.title: Then allow eating in the sixth hour too
steps.stepSummary: If the sun's position prevents mistakes between morning and afternoon, the sixth hour is still before noon ends. So רבי מאיר should allow eating חמץ in the sixth hour as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let him also eat in the sixth hour!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer in Step 8. If the sun tells the time so clearly, why forbid the sixth hour?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sun answer seems to prove too much. The sixth hour is also before the sun moves west, so it should not be confused with the seventh. Then the sixth hour should be allowed too.

phrases.english: If so, in the sixth too let him eat?!
phrases.notes: The sun answer seems to allow the sixth hour too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 8 by pushing it one hour further.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the sun's position prevents confusion with the seventh hour, the sixth hour should be just as safe. Yet רבי מאיר forbids it.

steps.title: At the sixth hour the sun stands at the top of the sky
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה answers that during the sixth hour the sun is right overhead, in the middle of the sky. You cannot tell if it is leaning east or west, so the sixth hour can be confused with the seventh.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: in the sixth hour, the sun stands at the 'corners' (the middle point of the sky).
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה explains why the sixth hour is different from the fifth. At noon the sun's direction is unclear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sun answer only works when the sun is clearly east or clearly west. Around the sixth hour it sits at the peak, and then it is hard to tell whether noon has passed. So רבי מאיר is right to forbid the sixth hour.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'corners' / the peak point of the sky, directly overhead

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי מאיר: the fifth hour is allowed because the sun is clearly in the east. The sixth hour is forbidden because the sun is overhead and could be confused with the seventh hour.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
In the sixth, the day stands at the meridian.
phrases.notes: The sun is directly overhead, so its direction is unclear.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה: שֵׁית, יוֹמָא בְּקַרְנָתָא קָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing a special case: the sixth hour is unclear in the sky
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sun's position makes every morning hour clearly different from the seventh hour.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the sixth hour the sun is at the peak, so it can be confused with the seventh. Only the fifth hour and earlier are clearly 'east'.

steps.title: If people err almost three hours, stop eating from the fourth hour
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's view of רבי יהודה. If a person can be off by almost three hours, someone in the fourth hour might really be in the seventh. So רבי יהודה should forbid eating from the start of the fourth hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבא's explanation of רבי יהודה, who said a person can err by three hours minus a little bit: then from the start of the fourth hour one should not eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now runs the same kind of challenge against רבא's explanation of רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה lets people eat through the fourth hour. An error of almost three hours could link the fourth hour to the seventh, which is forbidden by Torah law. So his margin seems one hour too short.

phrases.english: And Rava, according to Rabbi Yehuda,
who said: a person errs
by three hours less a bit —
from the beginning of the fourth, let him not eat!
phrases.notes: The fourth hour could be confused with the seventh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same pattern as Step 7, now aimed at רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that, according to רבי יהודה, a person errs by almost three hours
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An error of almost three hours links the fourth hour to the seventh. So eating should stop at the start of the fourth hour.

steps.title: The sun answer works even better for the fourth hour
steps.stepSummary: The same sun logic answers this question. If even the fifth hour, with the sun in the east, is not confused with the seventh, then surely the fourth hour is not, since the sun is even further east.
steps.simpleTranslation: At five the sun is in the east, and at seven the sun is in the west. All the more so at four.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reuses the sun answer and adds a כל שכן: the fourth hour is even easier to tell apart from the seventh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fifth hour already cannot be confused with the seventh. The fourth hour is earlier in the morning and even further from the afternoon. So the error of almost three hours does not reach the seventh hour.

keyTerms.meaning: And all the more so (a קל וחומר-style argument)

phrases.english: at five, the sun is in the east,
and at seven, the sun is in the west.
And all the more so four.
phrases.notes: At four the sun is even further east, so it is surely not confused with seven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 11 by applying the answer of Step 8 with a כל שכן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applying an earlier answer with an 'all the more so' argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An error of almost three hours could link the fourth hour to the seventh.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sun is clearly in the east at the fourth hour, so it cannot be confused with the seventh.

steps.title: Then רבי יהודה should allow eating in the fifth hour too
steps.stepSummary: If the sun's position keeps morning separate from afternoon, the fifth hour is also safe. So why does רבי יהודה forbid eating in the fifth hour?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let him also eat in the fifth hour!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the sun answer against רבי יהודה himself. The fifth hour is also clearly morning, so he should allow eating then.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 already said the fifth hour cannot be confused with the seventh. But רבי יהודה treats the fifth hour as 'in suspension' (תלויין) and forbids eating then. Step 14 answers this question.

keyTerms.meaning: 'In suspension': רבי יהודה's status for the fifth hour, when one may not eat חמץ but need not burn it yet

steps.confusionAlert: The next step answers this challenge. Do not think the sun answer settles רבי יהודה's view of the fifth hour. The גמרא still needs to explain it.

phrases.english: If so, in the fifth too let him eat!
phrases.notes: Since the fifth hour cannot be confused with the seventh, רבי יהודה should allow it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 12 by pushing it to the fifth hour, like Step 9 did for רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's ban on eating in the fifth hour, given the sun-position answer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The sun is clearly east at the fifth hour, so it cannot be confused with the seventh. Then רבי יהודה should allow eating in the fifth hour, but he does not.

steps.title: Testimony is for careful people, but חמץ is for everyone
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains, following רבא, that witnesses are careful people, but the rules of חמץ apply to everyone. So the רבנן were stricter with חמץ and forbade the fifth hour too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי explained it according to רבא: testimony is given to careful people, but חמץ is given to everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question from step 13 by contrasting witnesses with ordinary people who own חמץ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses in court are careful, alert people, so the sun reasoning works for them. The laws of חמץ apply to every Jew, including careless people who might confuse the fifth hour with the seventh. That is why the רבנן added the fifth hour as an extra safety buffer for חמץ.

phrases.english: Abaye explained it according to Rava:
Testimony is entrusted to the careful,
phrases.notes: Witnesses are careful people, so they do not make big mistakes about the time.

phrases.english: chametz is entrusted to everyone.
phrases.notes: Every person must deal with חמץ, even careless people, so the rule must be stricter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between two groups of people (careful witnesses compared with the general public)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sun reasoning that protects witnesses should protect everyone, so the fifth hour should be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: For חמץ, the רבנן worried about careless people too, so they also forbade the fifth hour.

steps.title: רבא's own reason: an hour to gather wood for burning
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the real reason for the fifth hour has nothing to do with mistakes. רבי יהודה holds that חמץ must be burned, so the רבנן gave an hour to gather wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: that is not רבי יהודה's reason. רבי יהודה follows his own opinion that חמץ may only be removed by burning, so the רבנן gave him one hour to gather wood.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects the whole 'people make mistakes' idea and gives a completely different reason for the fifth hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Elsewhere רבי יהודה rules that the only way to get rid of חמץ is to burn it. Burning needs wood, and finding wood takes time. So the extra hour is not a buffer against mistakes. It is a practical hour set aside for getting ready to burn.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
That is not the reason of Rabbi Yehuda.
Rather, Rabbi Yehuda follows his own reasoning,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אֵין בִּיעוּר חָמֵץ אֶלָּא שְׂרֵיפָה,
phrases.english: for he said: removal of chametz is only by burning,
and the Rabbis gave him one hour
in which to gather wood.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר: לָאו הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the question of step 13, rejecting the 'mistake' framework
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the underlying reason for the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fifth hour is forbidden because people might confuse the time.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fifth hour is forbidden so that people have time to gather wood for burning, since רבי יהודה requires burning.

steps.title: רבינא: at the deadline, any method of removal works
steps.stepSummary: רבינא quotes רבי יהודה himself: burning is only required before the deadline. At the deadline, you may destroy חמץ any way you like, so there is no need for an hour to gather wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא challenged רבא: רבי יהודה said, when does burning apply? Only when it is not the time for removal. But at the time for removal, you may destroy it in any way!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks רבא's 'wood-gathering hour' with a ברייתא quoting רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's answer depends on the idea that at the deadline you must burn, so you need wood. But רבי יהודה says that at the deadline itself, any method of destruction is fine. So nobody needs extra time to find wood, and רבא's reason falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him (from a source)
The time when it must be removed (the deadline)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי יהודה changed his mind about burning. Burning is still the ideal method. The ברייתא says only that at the actual deadline, when there is no time left, any method is acceptable.

phrases.english: Ravina raised an objection to Rava:
Rabbi Yehuda said: When (must it be burned)?
When it is not at its time of removal.
But at its time of removal,
its elimination may be done with anything!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the fifth hour is given to gather wood for burning
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה himself allows any method of destruction at the deadline, so no time is needed to gather wood.

steps.title: רבא's new reason: a decree because of cloudy days
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a new reason: the fifth hour is forbidden because of cloudy days. When the sun cannot be seen, the fifth hour could be confused with the seventh.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: it is a decree because of a cloudy day.
steps.whatsHappening: After his wood reason is rejected, רבא offers a new reason for forbidding the fifth hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 8 and 12 relied on seeing the sun in the east to tell morning from afternoon. On a cloudy day you cannot see the sun, so a person could mistake the fifth hour for the seventh. The רבנן made one rule for all days because of cloudy days.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made as a safeguard

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
It is a decree because of a cloudy day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: גְּזֵירָה מִשּׁוּם יוֹם הַמְעוּנָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 15 with a new answer to step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reason that removes the protection of the sun logic
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the sun shows morning and afternoon clearly, the fifth hour should be safe.
steps.terutzMaskana: On cloudy days the sun cannot be seen, so the fifth hour is forbidden as a safeguard.

steps.title: Then the fourth hour should be forbidden too
steps.stepSummary: If cloudy days are the concern, a person could be off by almost three hours. Then even the fourth hour could be confused with the seventh, so eating should be forbidden then too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even in the fourth hour he should not be allowed to eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's cloudy-day reason by pushing it one hour earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 protected the fourth hour by using the sun's position. On a cloudy day that protection is gone. With an error of almost three hours, the fourth hour could also be mistaken for the seventh.

phrases.english: If so,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ בְּאַרְבַּע שָׁעוֹת נָמֵי לָא נֵיכוֹל!
phrases.english: even in the fourth hour he should also not eat!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ בְּאַרְבַּע שָׁעוֹת נָמֵי לָא נֵיכוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in step 17
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without the sun, the error of almost three hours puts the fourth hour at risk too, so it should also be forbidden.

steps.title: The fourth hour is everyone's mealtime
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the fourth hour is the usual mealtime for everyone, so people know when it is and will not confuse it with another hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: the fourth hour is mealtime for everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא defends רבא's cloudy-day reason by showing why the fourth hour is still safe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even without the sun, people know the fourth hour because everyone eats then. That fixed daily habit acts like a clock. So the fourth hour is not confused with the seventh, but the fifth hour has no such marker and is forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: The final explanation for רבי יהודה (according to רבא): the fifth hour is forbidden because on a cloudy day it could be mistaken for the seventh. The fourth hour stays permitted because it is everyone's regular mealtime, so no one mistakes it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that people can keep track of time through regular daily habits, not only by looking at the sun.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
The fourth (hour) is mealtime for everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: אַרְבַּע זְמַן סְעוּדָה לַכֹּל הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 18
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing out a distinguishing feature of the fourth hour
steps.terutzHavaAmina: On a cloudy day the fourth hour could be confused just like the fifth.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fourth hour is known to all as mealtime, so it is not confused. Only the fifth hour needs the safeguard.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists who eats at each hour of the morning
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא describes which kind of person eats at each of the first six hours of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: The first hour is mealtime for the לודים (a wild, hungry people). The second is mealtime for robbers. The third is mealtime for rich heirs. The fourth is mealtime for workers. The fifth is mealtime for תלמידי חכמים. The sixth is mealtime for everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: Since רב פפא just mentioned the usual mealtime, the גמרא brings a ברייתא about mealtimes. It goes hour by hour and says who eats at each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier you eat, the less self-control the ברייתא suggests you have. Wild people, robbers who were up all night, and idle rich heirs eat early. Workers and scholars eat later, and the ordinary person eats at the sixth hour. Notice that this version puts everyone's mealtime at the sixth hour, not the fourth. That will cause a problem in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A wild people known for being ravenous
Heirs, wealthy people who do not need to work

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
The first hour is mealtime for the Ludim.
phrases.notes: A wild nation, always hungry and in a rush to eat.

phrases.english: The second is mealtime for robbers.
phrases.notes: They are up all night stealing, so they eat early.

phrases.english: The third is mealtime for heirs.
phrases.notes: They have no work to do, so they eat early.

phrases.english: The fourth is mealtime for workers.
The fifth is mealtime for Torah scholars.
The sixth is mealtime for all people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Prompted by רב פפא's mention of the fourth hour as the usual mealtime, the גמרא brings a related ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each hour from first to sixth is the mealtime of a different type of person, with the sixth listed as everyone's mealtime.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא said the fourth hour is everyone's mealtime, but the ברייתא gives the fourth hour to workers and the sixth to everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב פפא say that the fourth hour is mealtime for everyone?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא with what רב פפא just said in Step 19. The two sources do not match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא's answer in Step 19 depended on the fourth hour being the common mealtime, which is why no one would mix it up with another hour. The ברייתא, though, says the sixth hour is everyone's mealtime. If the ברייתא is right, רב פפא's answer is weakened.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (opens a challenge from another statement)

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Pappa say:
The fourth hour is mealtime for all!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא from Step 20 using רב פפא's statement from Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The order of hours in the ברייתא (Step 20)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב פפא says the fourth hour is the universal mealtime, but the ברייתא makes the sixth hour the universal mealtime. They cannot both be correct.

steps.title: Reverse the last three hours of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא's order: the fourth hour is for everyone, the fifth for workers, the sixth for scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, reverse it: the fourth hour is mealtime for everyone, the fifth is mealtime for workers, and the sixth is mealtime for תלמידי חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing the order of the ברייתא so it agrees with רב פפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only hours four through six are switched around. Everyone now eats at the fourth hour, which matches רב פפא. Workers eat at the fifth, and scholars, who are busy learning, eat last at the sixth.
steps.whatToRemember: The accepted order is: fourth hour, everyone; fifth hour, workers; sixth hour, תלמידי חכמים.

phrases.english: Rather, reverse it:
The fourth is mealtime for all people,
the fifth is mealtime for workers,
the sixth is mealtime for Torah scholars.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 21 by changing the text of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא says everyone eats at the sixth hour, which contradicts רב פפא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא should be read with the fourth hour for everyone, matching רב פפא.

steps.title: Eating after the sixth hour does no good
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: eating after the sixth hour is like throwing a stone into a leather bottle.
steps.simpleTranslation: From then on, eating is like throwing a stone into a leather bottle.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא goes on to say that eating a first meal later than the sixth hour does not help the body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A stone thrown into a leather water bottle does not fill it in any useful way. In the same way, food eaten this late does not nourish the person properly.

keyTerms.meaning: From here on, from this point forward

phrases.english: From here on,
it is like throwing a stone into a leather bottle.
phrases.notes: It brings no benefit to the body.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא after the order of hours was fixed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A first meal eaten after the sixth hour does not benefit the body.

steps.title: אביי limits the rule to someone who ate nothing in the morning
steps.stepSummary: אביי says late eating is useless only if the person tasted nothing in the morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We only said this when he did not taste anything in the morning. But if he tasted something in the morning, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי narrows the ברייתא's warning about eating late.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's warning applies only when the late meal is the first food of the day. If the person had a little something in the morning, a later meal still does him good.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when (introduces a limitation)
We have no problem with it

phrases.english: Abaye said:
We only said this
when he did not taste anything in the morning.
But if he tasted something in the morning,
we have no problem with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule stated in Step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating after the sixth hour is useless only for someone who ate nothing that morning.

steps.title: רב אשי: the dispute about witnesses matches the dispute about חמץ
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about חמץ the same way they argue about witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Just like the dispute about עדות, so is the dispute about חמץ.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the main topic of the daf. רב אשי makes a summary statement linking the two disputes of רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier on the דף, the גמרא saw that רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה disagree about how big a mistake witnesses make about the time. It looked like their positions on חמץ did not match their positions on witnesses. רב אשי declares that the two disputes really do line up.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Like the dispute regarding testimony,
so is the dispute regarding chametz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the mealtime discussion and returns to the main sugya about רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה are consistent: their dispute in עדות parallels their dispute in חמץ.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious from what we already said?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב אשי adds, since the earlier answers already showed the two disputes match.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious! This is exactly what we already said!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אשי's statement as unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole back-and-forth on the דף already reconciled the two disputes. So saying they match seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (asks why a statement is needed)
This is the same as that

phrases.english: It is obvious!
This is exactly what we said!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why רב אשי's statement in Step 25 is needed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The earlier answers already showed the disputes line up, so the statement seems redundant.

steps.title: The earlier answers are real answers
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי teaches that the reconciling answers are true explanations, not forced ones covering up a dispute between תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he teaches us: The answers we gave are real answers. Do not say that this is really a dispute between תנאים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רב אשי adds, and this closes the discussion reconciling עדות and חמץ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think the earlier answers were only a stretch. Then the real explanation would be that different תנאים reported רבי מאיר's and רבי יהודה's views differently. רב אשי tells us the answers are correct, so each Sage truly holds one consistent view.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he teaches us
An answer that resolves a contradiction
It is a dispute between תנאים

steps.whatToRemember: The final word: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה are each consistent between עדות and חמץ. The distinctions made earlier on the דף are genuine explanations, not a cover for a hidden dispute between תנאים.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't misread 'פשיטא' as rejecting רב אשי. The גמרא just asks what he adds, then shows his real point: the earlier answers are real answers.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the גמרא treats its own answers. A שינויא can be a true explanation of the Sages' views, not just a way to escape a question.

phrases.english: This is what he teaches us:
the answers that we answered are real answers,
and do not say it is a dispute of Tannaim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of Step 26 by identifying רב אשי's real point.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the new information in the statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The earlier answers might have been forced, with the real explanation being a dispute between תנאים about what רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה held.
steps.terutzMaskana: The earlier answers are genuine, so each Sage is consistent between עדות and חמץ.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה each hold one consistent view in עדות and חמץ, and the reconciling answers on the דף are real explanations.

steps.title: Hour differences are forgiven, but a sunrise difference voids the testimony
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי says the leniency for witnesses who disagree about the time applies only to differences in hours. If one witness says 'before sunrise' and the other says 'after sunrise,' their testimony is cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: They only taught this about hours. But if one says 'before sunrise' and the other says 'after sunrise,' their testimony is void.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר אשי sets a limit on the earlier rule that witnesses who disagree by about an hour are still believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People can easily mix up which hour it was, so a small gap in hours is treated as an honest mistake. Sunrise, however, is a clear and visible event. A disagreement about whether something happened before or after sunrise is a real contradiction, and it cancels the testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this rule in the case of… (a limiting formula)

steps.whyThisMatters: It draws a line between a forgivable estimation error and a real contradiction between witnesses.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
They only taught this regarding hours,
phrases.notes: That is, the rule that a time discrepancy does not cancel testimony.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֶחָד אוֹמֵר קוֹדֶם הָנֵץ הַחַמָּה
phrases.english: but if one says before sunrise
and one says after sunrise —
their testimony is void.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּשָׁעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the parallel between the two disputes to a limit on how far witness discrepancies are tolerated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The tolerance for time discrepancies covers only differences in hours. A before-sunrise versus after-sunrise discrepancy voids the testimony.

steps.title: This is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רב שימי בר אשי's case does not need to be said, because before and after sunrise are obviously different.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב שימי בר אשי by saying his ruling teaches nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one could confuse a time before sunrise with a time after it, because the difference is plain to see. A teaching that only states the obvious seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious (a challenge that a statement adds nothing)

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the statement in Step 28 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב שימי בר אשי's case of before sunrise versus after sunrise.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The contradiction is so clear that no sage needed to teach it.

steps.title: The statement is reworded to before sunrise versus during sunrise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording of the statement: the real case is one witness saying 'before sunrise' and the other saying 'during sunrise.' Even then, the testimony is void.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the statement is: if one says 'before sunrise' and one says 'during sunrise,' their testimony is void.
steps.whatsHappening: To answer the 'obvious' objection, the גמרא rewords רב שימי בר אשי's case so the two times are closer together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Before sunrise' and 'during sunrise' are much closer than 'before' and 'after.' This makes the ruling more of a חידוש. Even this small gap counts as a real contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: During sunrise, as the sun is coming up

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not adding a second case. It replaces the 'after sunrise' version with the 'during sunrise' version.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא: אֶחָד אוֹמֵר קוֹדֶם הָנֵץ הַחַמָּה
phrases.english: Rather: one says before sunrise
and one says during sunrise —
their testimony is void.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: אֶחָד אוֹמֵר קוֹדֶם הָנֵץ הַחַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by rewording the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The statement was about before versus after sunrise, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The statement is about before versus during sunrise, a closer gap that still voids the testimony.

steps.title: The reworded case is also obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that even the reworded case seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: This too is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back again and says the new version still teaches nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even 'before sunrise' versus 'during sunrise' seems like a clear difference that anyone would notice. So the challenge from Step 29 returns against the new wording.

phrases.english: This too is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the 'obvious' objection against the reworded case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reworded case of before sunrise versus during sunrise.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The difference between these two times is still clearly visible, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Why the ruling is needed: we might think both witnesses mean the same moment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to explain why the ruling is needed. Without it, we might have thought both witnesses are describing the same moment in different words. This passage ends in the middle of this explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: both of them are saying one thing, and the one who says…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts its answer by describing the mistaken assumption the ruling comes to correct. The rest of the sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'you might have thought' is that the two witnesses do not really disagree. They both mean the same moment, and their different wording can be explained away. רב שימי בר אשי teaches that we do not reconcile them this way, and the testimony is void.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introducing a mistaken assumption that a ruling corrects)

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is cut off at the end of the עמוד. The explanation of why the second witness said 'during sunrise' continues on the next עמוד.

phrases.english: You might have said:
both of them are saying one thing,
and the fact that the one says
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: תַּרְוַיְיהוּ חֲדָא מִילְּתָא קָאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second 'obvious' challenge by showing there was a reasonable assumption to correct.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא — showing the ruling corrects a reasonable mistake
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both witnesses are describing the same moment, and their different wording can be reconciled.
steps.terutzMaskana: (Completed on the next amud) We do not reconcile them, and the testimony is void.
